messages.content: How far will a car travel in time 't' when launched with velocity 'v' at an angle 'theta'?

function.name: calculate_projectile_range
function.description: Calculate the range of a projectile launched at an angle with initial velocity, using the kinematic equation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity at which projectile is launched. This is a float type value.

angle.description: The angle at which projectile is launched. This should be in degrees. This is a float type value.

time.description: The time in seconds after which the range is to be calculated. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Answer**

For a projectile (or a “car” that is launched into the air) the motion can be split into horizontal and vertical components.  
Let  

* \(v\) – initial speed (m s⁻¹)  
* \(\theta\) – launch angle measured from the horizontal (degrees or radians)  
* \(t\) – elapsed time after launch (s)  
* \(g \approx 9.81\;\text{m s}^{-2}\) – acceleration due to gravity (downward)

---

### 1. Horizontal distance travelled in a given time \(t\)

The horizontal component of the velocity is constant (ignoring air resistance):

\[
v_x = v \cos\theta
\]

Hence the horizontal displacement after time \(t\) is

\[
\boxed{\,x(t) = v \cos\theta \; t\,}
\]

If you only care about how far the car has moved along the ground (i.e., the *range*), this is the quantity you need.

---

### 2. Vertical displacement after time \(t\)

The vertical component of the velocity changes under gravity:

\[
v_y(t) = v \sin\theta - g t
\]

The vertical position relative to the launch point is

\[
\boxed{\,y(t) = v \sin\theta \; t \;-\; \tfrac12 g t^2\,}
\]

---

### 3. Total straight‑line distance from the launch point

If you want the straight‑line (Euclidean) distance from the launch point to the car’s position at time \(t\), combine the two components:

\[
\boxed{\,d(t) = \sqrt{\,\bigl(v \cos\theta \; t\bigr)^2 \;+\; \bigl(v \sin\theta \; t - \tfrac12 g t^2\bigr)^2\,}\;}
\]

---

### 4. Special case: distance when the car lands (range)

When the car returns to the launch height (\(y=0\)), the flight time is

\[
t_{\text{flight}} = \frac{2 v \sin\theta}{g}
\]

Plugging this into the horizontal distance gives the classic range formula:

\[
\boxed{\,R = \frac{v^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}\,}
\]

---

#### Quick reference

| Quantity | Formula |
|----------|---------|
| Horizontal distance after time \(t\) | \(x(t)=v\cos\theta\,t\) |
| Vertical distance after time \(t\) | \(y(t)=v\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12gt^2\) |
| Straight‑line distance after time \(t\) | \(d(t)=\sqrt{[v\cos\theta\,t]^2+[v\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12gt^2]^2}\) |
| Range (when landing) | \(R=\dfrac{v^2\sin(2\theta)}{g}\) |

---

**Example**

Suppose a car is launched at \(v = 20\;\text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(\theta = 30^\circ\).  
After \(t = 3\;\text{s}\):

* \(x(3) = 20 \cos 30^\circ \times 3 \approx 51.96\;\text{m}\)
* \(y(3) = 20 \sin 30^\circ \times 3 - 0.5 \times 9.81 \times 3^2 \approx 30 - 44.145 \approx -14.15\;\text{m}\) (below launch level)
* \(d(3) \approx \sqrt{51.96^2 + (-14.15)^2} \approx 53.6\;\text{m}\)

If you want the total distance until the car lands, compute \(t_{\text{flight}} = 2 v \sin\theta / g \approx 2.04\;\text{s}\) and then \(R \approx 20^2 \sin 60^\circ / 9.81 \approx 68.8\;\text{m}\).

Feel free to plug in your own numbers!
